title: Additive Huber 360 training in rehabilitation after acute ankle sprain: effects on objective functional parameters and patient-reported outcomes – a prospective controlled pilot study
summary:
Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries in sports and everyday life. Although many of these injuries can be treated without surgery, some patients experience persistent symptoms, insecurity during walking, or difficulties returning to sport. This study investigates whether additional structured training using a specialized training and diagnostic system can improve rehabilitation after an acute ankle sprain.
Physically active adults aged 18 to 35 years with an acute lateral ankle ligament injury may participate if surgical treatment is not required. One group receives standard treatment with bracing and physiotherapy. A second group receives additional training using the Huber 360 system. This training focuses on balance, stability, coordination, and strength. In addition, a group of healthy physically active adults is assessed to help interpret the functional measurement results.
Functional assessments and questionnaires are performed at the start of rehabilitation, after completion of the rehabilitation phase, and after approximately six months. The aim is to determine whether the additional training can improve ankle function, perceived stability, and return to physical activity.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Physically active adults aged 18 to 35 years are eligible for inclusion. For the patient groups, additional inclusion criteria are: acute lateral ankle sprain with a conservatively treatable lateral ligament injury, inclusion within 7–10 days after injury, physical activity before injury, and ability to provide informed consent. For the healthy comparison cohort, additional inclusion criteria are: no acute ankle injury, no relevant musculoskeletal pre-existing conditions, no pain at rest, and physical activity.
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria are injuries requiring surgical treatment, in particular open injuries, relevant osteochondral fractures or other severe concomitant injuries, previous relevant injuries or surgery of the affected ankle, chronic musculoskeletal disorders, relevant neurological or internal medical conditions, regular medication with a potential influence on training or outcomes, inability to provide informed consent, and lack of willingness or ability to attend the scheduled assessment and training appointments.
